I have discovered that the hevea package in Fedora also uses a QPL license modified to choose France instead of Norway.

- [Project home page](http://hevea.inria.fr/)
- [License file](https://github.com/maranget/hevea/blob/master/LICENSE)

@swinslow - I'm thinking that choice of law needs to be a different license, agree? 
In which case, we could call it: QPL-1.0-France ?

But I also noticed this exception text at the top:
` As a special exception to the Q Public Licence, you may develop
  application programs, reusable components and other software items
  that link with the original or modified versions of the Software
  and are not made available to the general public, without any of the
  additional requirements listed in clause 6c of the Q Public licence.`

@jamesjer - have you seen that before?
edited - I've answered my own question (no wonder this was familiar...) https://gitlab.com/fedora/legal/fedora-license-data/-/issues/84

need to add a submission for the exception too
I've added the exception as a separate request #1746

@swinslow For the identifier, I would argue for either "QPL-1.0-OCaml" or "QPL-1.0-INRIA". 

Some background: OCaml is a project stewarded by INRIA. HEVEA is apparently also an INRIA project written in OCaml. The LICENSE file for HEVEA is kind of confusing but without checking I think they may have just copied over the old LICENSE file of the OCaml implementation. It is not clear whether HEVEA chose to use the (modified) QPL because of the familiar tendency to use the license of the language ("same as Ruby" and so forth) or because of some perceived copyleft obligation, or both; maybe it doesn't matter. OCaml itself ceased using the (modified) QPL a number of years ago, but there are apparently a number of OCaml projects besides HEVEA using old, pre-license-change source code from OCaml. HEVEA may be the only remaining project that appears to use the OCaml QPL as a main project license as opposed to a license for isolated source files, but no one has done the research into this. 

It seems most appropriate for the identifier to refer to the original project that used this QPL variant (OCaml, which is a fairly well known project, whereas I suspect HEVEA is relatively obscure) or to the license steward, if you will, for the QPL variant or the project steward for OCaml (both past and preent) as well as for HEVEA: INRIA. On the other hand, having the identifier refer to one minor project that may only be using it because they didn't know that OCaml had relicensed (I mean, this seems possible), seems less justifiable to me. 

I think using "QPL-" in the name is also justified, because up until @jamesjer submitted the corresponding Fedora gitlab issue, FOSS license trivia enthusiasts (like me) were assuming that the old OCaml license *was* the "real" QPL, identical to the once-famous old Trolltech Qt license; that the story was, the QPL had been abandoned by Trolltech but picked up later on, bizarrely, by the OCaml project. (In retrospect, I should have checked; I was well aware of the picturesque reference to the Oslo City Court in the original QPL and it would have been astounding if a French government research institute would have used a license with that choice of law/venue clause.) This seems to me no worse than all the many SPDX identifiers that refer to "MIT" and "BSD" for licenses with no historical connection to MIT or UC Berkeley, above all in the case of 0BSD where the license isn't even a textual descendant of any Berkeley-associated license. There are probably many other such examples in the SPDX license list. 

BTW: based on a quick Sourcegraph search I count about 7 or so Fedora OCaml packages today that are using Callaway (pre-SPDX) "QPL" in package license metadata.

Thanks @richardfontana! Appreciate the details here  😄 

This sent me digging a bit deeper, and it looks like the OCaml compiler went through [several license iterations itself](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/commits/cc0f32b05439bb7018e8ad62a54d6371b01aab9f/LICENSE). Here's a brief run-down of the major points, though I'm not sure this is even a complete list:
* [1995](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/blob/59cf50795583b4308a541ab85bd636ddfc9042ce/LICENSE): earliest license in Git commit history. INRIA custom license, limiting modifications to personal use and containing some other restrictions
* [1999](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/blob/cc0f32b05439bb7018e8ad62a54d6371b01aab9f/LICENSE): switched to QPL + LGPL. Note that this QPL instance has France for choice of law _and Versailles specified as venue for disputes_; it looks like [HEVEA also had this clause at the time](https://github.com/maranget/hevea/commit/e925fbe53a42751a585b3fa448684349530368c7).
* [2001](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/commit/02ef950033b81fe371759f024faa55f361ba83a6): added an LGPL exception (I haven't looked at this closely; it is modified in later commits)
* [2004](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/blob/c3a39fc8c84698aa4985c779e16493c2409a0285/LICENSE): added a note about changing the QPL's choice of law; added a QPL exception; and removed Versailles venue. _At this point, I believe it now matches the HEVEA license we're discussing in this thread. HEVEA seems to have made corresponding changes [in 2005](https://github.com/maranget/hevea/commit/ae61e4da4d895d2f312fc3901da31d86e55b8845)._
* [2016](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/blob/7fc2d214c4ee8853615fc3e5649f45e11d85378d/LICENSE): removed QPL and QPL exception; modified LGPL exception (which is currently on the SPDX License List as [`OCaml-LGPL-linking-exception`](https://spdx.org/licenses/OCaml-LGPL-linking-exception.html), discussed in #649)

This might all be a bit of a needless tangent :grin: but it suggests to me that perhaps the right ID and name could be:

* ID: QPL-1.0-INRIA-2004
* name: Q Public License 1.0 - INRIA 2004 variant

because it's possible that someone will want the 1999 variant someday...
